results.title: python - asyncio.gather vs asyncio.wait (vs asyncio.TaskGroup) - Stack Overflow
results.snippet: @EigenFool As of Python 3.9, asyncio.wait has a parameter called return_when, which you can use to control when the event loop should yield back to you. asyncio.gather does not have such parameter, the event loop only get back to you when all tasks have finished/failed.

results.title: Waiting in asyncio
results.snippet: If you now think that there would be no need for wait_for() if gather() had a timeout option, we’re thinking the same thing. Takes one awaitable. Wraps the awaitable in a task if necessary. Takes a timeout that cancels the task if it expires. Unlike create_task(), is a coroutine itself that doesn’t execute until awaited. Since Python 3.11, a more elegant approach to timeouts are asyncio.timeout() and asyncio.timeout_at().

results.title: Creating and Managing Tasks with Asyncio - DEV Community
results.snippet: asyncio.wait: when you need to handle multiple tasks and want to track which tasks are completed and which are still pending. It's useful when you care about the status of each task separately. asyncio.gather: when you want to run multiple tasks concurrently and need the results in a list, especially when the order of results matters or you need to handle exceptions gracefully.
